metadata.title: Efficient Decision-Making by Volume-Conserving Physical Object

nodes.name: Multi-armed bandit problem (MBP)
nodes.statement: Suppose there are $M$ slot machines, each of which returns a reward; for example, a coin, with a certain probability that is unknown to a player. Let us consider a minimal case: two machines A and B give rewards with individual probabilities $P_A$ and $P_B$, respectively. The player makes a decision on which machine to play at each trial, trying to maximize the total reward obtained after repeating several trials. The multi-armed bandit problem (MBP) is used to determine the optimal strategy for finding the machine with the highest reward probability as accurately and quickly as possible by referring to past experiences.
nodes.statement_short: Find the highest-reward-probability slot machine as accurately and quickly as possible while maximizing total reward.

nodes.name: Breadth of MBP applications
nodes.statement: The MBP is formulated as a mathematical problem without loss of generality and so is related to various stochastic phenomena. In fact, many application problems in diverse fields, such as communications (cognitive networks~\cite{cog,cog2}), commerce (advertising on the web~\cite{web}), entertainment (Monte-Carlo tree search, which is used for computer games~\cite{uct,mogo}), and so on, can be reduced to MBPs.
nodes.statement_short: Many practical problems in communications, commerce and game search reduce to MBPs.
nodes.origin_citation: Lai et al.; Agarwal et al.; Kocsis & Szepesvari; Gelly et al.

nodes.name: upper confidence bound 1 (UCB1) algorithm
nodes.statement: Particularly, the ``upper confidence bound 1 (UCB1) algorithm'' for solving MBPs is used worldwide in many practical applications~\cite{auer}.
nodes.statement_short: UCB1: the widely deployed index-based baseline policy for MBPs.

nodes.name: Gittins index
nodes.statement: The optimal strategy, called the ``Gittins index'', is known only for a limited class of problems in which the reward distributions are assumed to be known to the players~\cite{gittins1,gittins2}. Even in this limited class, in practice, computing the Gittins index becomes intractable for many cases.
nodes.statement_short: The optimal Gittins-index strategy is known only for restricted, known-distribution problems and is computationally intractable in practice.

nodes.name: Volume conservation enables efficient decision-making
nodes.statement: In this Letter, we show that a physical constraint, the conservation law for the volume of a rigid body, allows for efficient solving of decision-making problems when subjected to suitable operations involving fluctuations.
nodes.statement_short: The volume-conservation constraint of a rigid body, plus fluctuating operations, yields efficient decision-making.
assumptions: a physical constraint, the conservation law for the volume of a rigid body
when subjected to suitable operations involving fluctuations
conclusions: allows for efficient solving of decision-making problems

nodes.name: Amoeba-inspired origin of tug-of-war (TOW) dynamics
nodes.statement: Kim et al. proposed an MBP solution using a dynamical system, called ``tug-of-war (TOW) dynamics''; this algorithm was inspired by the spatiotemporal dynamics of a single-celled amoeboid organism (the true slime mold {\it P. polycephalum})~\cite{kim1,kim2,kim3,kim4,kim5,kim6}, which maintains a constant intracellular-resource volume while collecting environmental information by concurrently expanding and shrinking its pseudopod-like terminal parts. In this nature-inspired algorithm, the decision-making function is derived from its underlying physics, resembling that of a tug-of-war game.
nodes.statement_short: TOW dynamics was abstracted from the constant-volume pseudopod dynamics of the slime mold P. polycephalum.

nodes.name: Nonlocal correlation from the volume-conservation law
nodes.statement: The physical constraint in TOW dynamics, the conservation law for the volume of the amoeboid body, entails a nonlocal correlation among the terminal parts, that is, the volume increment in one part is immediately compensated by volume decrement(s) in the other part(s).
nodes.genus: a nonlocal correlation among the terminal parts
differentia: the volume increment in one part is immediately compensated by volume decrement(s) in the other part(s)

nodes.name: Higher performance of TOW dynamics in previous studies
nodes.statement: In our previous studies~\cite{kim1,kim2,kim3,kim4,kim5,kim6}, we showed that, owing to the nonlocal correlation derived from the volume-conservation law, TOW dynamics exhibit higher performance than other well-known algorithms such as the modified $\epsilon$-greedy algorithm and the modified softmax algorithm, which is comparable to the UCB1-tuned algorithm (seen as the best choice among parameter-free algorithms~\cite{auer}). These observations suggest that efficient decision-making devices could be implemented using any physical object as long as it held some common physical attributes such as the conservation law.
nodes.statement_short: TOW beats modified $\epsilon$-greedy and softmax and matches UCB1-tuned, suggesting any conservation-law object could serve as a decision-making device.
nodes.origin_citation: Kim, Aono & Hara 2010--2014 (kim1--kim6); Auer et al. 2002
assumptions: owing to the nonlocal correlation derived from the volume-conservation law
conclusions: TOW dynamics exhibit higher performance than other well-known algorithms such as the modified $\epsilon$-greedy algorithm and the modified softmax algorithm, which is comparable to the UCB1-tuned algorithm
efficient decision-making devices could be implemented using any physical object as long as it held some common physical attributes such as the conservation law

nodes.name: Quantum-dot implementation of TOW dynamics
nodes.statement: In fact, Kim et al. demonstrated that optical energy-transfer dynamics between quantum dots, in which energy is conserved, can be exploited for the implementation of TOW dynamics~\cite{QDM,QDM2}.
nodes.origin_citation: Kim et al. 2013; Naruse et al. 2014

nodes.name: Displacement $X_k$ of a volume-conserving physical object
nodes.statement: Consider a volume-conserving physical object; for example, a rigid body like an iron bar (the slot-machine's handle), as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:stow}. Here, the variable $X_k$ represents the displacement of terminal $k$ from an initial position, where $k\in \{A,B\}$. If $X_k$ is a maximum, we assume that the body makes a decision to play machine $k$.
nodes.statement_short: $X_k$ is the displacement of terminal $k$ of a volume-conserving rigid body; the maximal $X_k$ selects machine $k$.
nodes.genus: the displacement of terminal $k$ from an initial position
differentia: If $X_k$ is a maximum, we assume that the body makes a decision to play machine $k$

nodes.name: tug-of-war (TOW) dynamics
nodes.statement: In TOW dynamics, the MBP is represented in its inverse form: instead of ``rewarding'' the player when machine $k$ produces a coin with a probability $P_k$, we ``punish'' the player when the machine gives no coin with a probability $1 - P_k$. In this respect, the displacement $X_A$ ($= - X_B$) is determined by the following equations: \begin{eqnarray} X_A(t) & = & Q_A(t) - Q_B(t) + \delta(t) ,\\ Q_k(t) & = & N_k - (1 + \omega)\hspace{1mm}L_k . \end{eqnarray} Here, $Q_k(t)$ ($k\in \{A,B\}$) is an ``estimate'' of information on past experiences accumulated from the initial time $1$ to current time $t$, $N_k$ counts the number of times that machine $k$ has been played, $L_k$ counts the number of punishments when playing machine $k$, $\delta(t)$ is an arbitrary fluctuation to which the body is subjected, and $\omega$ is a weighting parameter to be described in detail later on in this Letter. Eq.(\ref{eq:org}), called the ``learning rule'', reflects the volume-conservation law. Consequently the TOW dynamics evolve according to a particularly simple rule: in addition to the fluctuation, if machine $k$ is played at each time $t$, $+1$ and $-\omega$ are added to $X_k(t-1)$ when rewarded and non-rewarded, respectively (Fig.~\ref{fig:stow}).
nodes.statement_short: Play the machine whose terminal displacement is largest, where the displacement is driven by the punishment-weighted learning rule $Q_k = N_k - (1+\omega)L_k$ plus a fluctuation.
input: $N_k$ counts the number of times that machine $k$ has been played
$L_k$ counts the number of punishments when playing machine $k$
$\delta(t)$ is an arbitrary fluctuation to which the body is subjected
$\omega$ is a weighting parameter to be described in detail later on in this Letter
output: an ``estimate'' of information on past experiences accumulated from the initial time $1$ to current time $t$

nodes.name: Displacement from the estimate difference
nodes.statement: X_A(t) & = & Q_A(t) - Q_B(t) + \delta(t) ,
nodes.statement_short: Set the terminal displacement to the estimate difference plus the fluctuation.

nodes.name: learning rule
nodes.statement: Q_k(t) & = & N_k - (1 + \omega)\hspace{1mm}L_k .
nodes.statement_short: Update each estimate by plays minus $(1+\omega)$ times punishments.

nodes.name: Reward / punishment increment
nodes.statement: in addition to the fluctuation, if machine $k$ is played at each time $t$, $+1$ and $-\omega$ are added to $X_k(t-1)$ when rewarded and non-rewarded, respectively
nodes.statement_short: Add $+1$ on a reward and $-\omega$ on a non-reward to the played terminal.

nodes.name: Random-walk model
nodes.statement: To explore the origins of the high performance of TOW dynamics, let us consider a random-walk model for comparison. As shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:random}(a), $\alpha$ (right flight when rewarded) and $\beta$ (left flight when non-rewarded) are the parameters. We assume that $P_A$ $>$ $P_B$ for simplicity. After time step $t$, the displacement $R_k(t)$ ($k\in \{A,B\}$) can be described by \begin{eqnarray} R_k(t) & = & \alpha (N_k - L_k) - \beta \hspace{1mm}L_k  \nonumber \\ & = & \alpha N_k - (\alpha + \beta)\hspace{1mm}L_k . \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: A comparison random walk with right flight $\alpha$ on a reward and left flight $\beta$ on a non-reward, giving displacement $R_k = \alpha N_k - (\alpha+\beta)L_k$.
differentia: $\alpha$ (right flight when rewarded) and $\beta$ (left flight when non-rewarded) are the parameters

nodes.name: Expected displacement of the random walk
nodes.statement: The expected value of $R_k$ can be obtained from the following equation: \begin{equation} E( R_k(t) ) = \{\alpha P_k - \beta (1 - P_k)\}\hspace{1mm} N_k . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The mean displacement grows linearly in $N_k$ with slope $\alpha P_k - \beta(1-P_k)$.

nodes.name: Ordering of the reward probabilities
nodes.statement: We assume that $P_A$ $>$ $P_B$ for simplicity.

nodes.name: Admissible range of the flight ratio $\beta/(\alpha+\beta)$
nodes.statement: In the overlapping area between the two distributions shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:random}(b), we cannot accurately estimate which is larger. The overlapping area should decrease as $N_k$ increases so as to avoid incorrect judgments. This requirement can be expressed by the following forms: \begin{eqnarray} \alpha P_A - \beta (1 - P_A) & > & 0 ,  \\ \alpha P_B - \beta (1 - P_B) & < & 0 . \end{eqnarray} These expressions can be rearranged into the form \begin{equation} P_B  < \frac{\beta}{\alpha + \beta}   < P_A . \end{equation} In other words, the parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$ must satisfy the above conditions so that the random walk correctly represents the larger judgment.
nodes.statement_short: Correct discrimination requires the flight ratio $\beta/(\alpha+\beta)$ to lie strictly between $P_B$ and $P_A$.
assumptions: We assume that $P_A$ $>$ $P_B$ for simplicity.
The overlapping area should decrease as $N_k$ increases so as to avoid incorrect judgments.
conclusions: the parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$ must satisfy the above conditions so that the random walk correctly represents the larger judgment

nodes.name: Derivation of the weighting parameter $\omega_0$
nodes.statement: We can easily confirm that the following form satisfies the above conditions: \begin{equation} \frac{\beta}{\alpha + \beta}   = \frac{P_A + P_B}{2} . \end{equation} From $R_k(t)/\alpha $ $=$ $Q_k(t)$, we obtain $\omega = \frac{\beta}{\alpha}$. From this and Eq.(\ref{eq:fixed}), we obtain \begin{eqnarray} \omega_0 & = & \frac{\gamma}{2 - \gamma} , \\ \gamma & = & P_A + P_B . \end{eqnarray} Here, we have set the parameter $\omega$ to $\omega_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick the midpoint $\beta/(\alpha+\beta) = (P_A+P_B)/2$ inside the admissible interval, then substitute $\omega = \beta/\alpha$ to get $\omega_0 = \gamma/(2-\gamma)$.

nodes.name: Choose the midpoint flight ratio
nodes.statement: We can easily confirm that the following form satisfies the above conditions: \begin{equation} \frac{\beta}{\alpha + \beta}   = \frac{P_A + P_B}{2} . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Exhibit a ratio inside the admissible interval: the mean of $P_A$ and $P_B$.

nodes.name: Identify $\omega$ with $\beta/\alpha$
nodes.statement: From $R_k(t)/\alpha $ $=$ $Q_k(t)$, we obtain $\omega = \frac{\beta}{\alpha}$.
nodes.statement_short: Rescale the random walk by $\alpha$ to match the TOW learning rule, giving $\omega = \beta/\alpha$.

nodes.name: Solve for $\omega_0$ in terms of $\gamma$
nodes.statement: From this and Eq.(\ref{eq:fixed}), we obtain \begin{eqnarray} \omega_0 & = & \frac{\gamma}{2 - \gamma} , \\ \gamma & = & P_A + P_B . \end{eqnarray} Here, we have set the parameter $\omega$ to $\omega_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $\omega_0 = \gamma/(2-\gamma)$ with $\gamma = P_A + P_B$.

nodes.name: Correctness of the learning rule $Q_k$ with $\omega_0$
nodes.statement: Therefore, we can conclude that the algorithm using the learning rule $Q_k$ with the parameter $\omega_0$ can solve the MBP correctly.
assumptions: $\frac{\beta}{\alpha + \beta}   = \frac{P_A + P_B}{2}$
Here, we have set the parameter $\omega$ to $\omega_0$.
conclusions: the algorithm using the learning rule $Q_k$ with the parameter $\omega_0$ can solve the MBP correctly

nodes.name: Known sum of reward probabilities $\gamma$
nodes.statement: In many popular algorithms such as the $\epsilon$-greedy algorithm, at each time $t$, an estimate of reward probability is updated for either of the two machines being played. On the other hand, in an imaginary circumstance in which the sum of the reward probabilities $\gamma$ $=$ $P_A$ $+$ $P_B$ is known to the player, we can update both of the two estimates simultaneously, even though only one of the machines was played.
nodes.statement_short: Assume the player knows $\gamma = P_A + P_B$, which allows both estimates to be updated after a single play.

nodes.name: Estimates for each reward probability under known $\gamma$
nodes.statement: Estimates for each reward probability based on the knowledge that machine $A$ was played $N_A$ times and that machine $B$ was played $N_B$ times---on the assumption that the sum of the reward probabilities $\gamma$ $=$ $P_A$ $+$ $P_B$ is known.
differentia: based on the knowledge that machine $A$ was played $N_A$ times and that machine $B$ was played $N_B$ times
on the assumption that the sum of the reward probabilities $\gamma$ $=$ $P_A$ $+$ $P_B$ is known

nodes.name: Updating the estimate of the unplayed machine
nodes.statement: The top and bottom rows of Table~\ref{table:1} provide estimates based on the knowledge that machine $A$ was played $N_A$ times and that machine $B$ was played $N_B$ times, respectively. Note that we can also update the estimate of the machine that was not played, owing to the given $\gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: Knowing $\gamma$ lets the unplayed machine's estimate be updated too.

nodes.name: Derivation of the equivalence between the TOW learning rule and the imaginary system
nodes.statement: From the above estimates, each expected reward $Q^{\prime}_k$ ($k\in \{A,B\}$) is given as follows: \begin{eqnarray} Q^{\prime}_A & = & N_A \hspace{1mm} \frac{N_A - L_A}{N_A} + N_B \hspace{1mm} \bigl( \gamma \hspace{1mm} - \frac{N_B - L_B}{N_B} \bigr) \nonumber \\ & = & N_A - L_A + (\gamma - 1) \hspace{1mm} N_B + L_B, \\ Q^{\prime}_B & = & N_A\hspace{1mm} \bigl( \gamma \hspace{1mm} - \frac{N_A - L_A}{N_A} \bigr) + N_B\hspace{1mm} \frac{N_B - L_B}{N_B} \nonumber \\ & = & N_B - L_B + (\gamma - 1) \hspace{1mm} N_A + L_A. \end{eqnarray} These expected rewards, $Q^{\prime}_j$s, are not the same as those given by the learning rules of TOW dynamics, $Q_j$s in Eq.(\ref{eq:org}). However, what we use substantially in TOW dynamics is the difference \begin{equation} Q_A - Q_B  =  (N_A - N_B) - (1 + \omega)\hspace{1mm}(L_A - L_B). \end{equation} When we transform the expected rewards $Q^{\prime}_j$s into $Q^{\prime \prime}_j  =  Q^{\prime}_j / (2 - \gamma)$, we can obtain the difference \begin{equation} Q^{\prime \prime}_A - Q^{\prime \prime}_B  =  (N_A - N_B) - \frac{2}{2-\gamma} \hspace{1mm} (L_A - L_B). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Compute the imaginary system's expected rewards, rescale them by $1/(2-\gamma)$, and compare the resulting difference term-by-term with the TOW difference $Q_A - Q_B$.

nodes.name: Expected rewards of the imaginary system
nodes.statement: From the above estimates, each expected reward $Q^{\prime}_k$ ($k\in \{A,B\}$) is given as follows: \begin{eqnarray} Q^{\prime}_A & = & N_A \hspace{1mm} \frac{N_A - L_A}{N_A} + N_B \hspace{1mm} \bigl( \gamma \hspace{1mm} - \frac{N_B - L_B}{N_B} \bigr) \nonumber \\ & = & N_A - L_A + (\gamma - 1) \hspace{1mm} N_B + L_B, \\ Q^{\prime}_B & = & N_A\hspace{1mm} \bigl( \gamma \hspace{1mm} - \frac{N_A - L_A}{N_A} \bigr) + N_B\hspace{1mm} \frac{N_B - L_B}{N_B} \nonumber \\ & = & N_B - L_B + (\gamma - 1) \hspace{1mm} N_A + L_A. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Expand the simultaneously-updated estimates into closed-form expected rewards $Q'_A$, $Q'_B$.

nodes.name: Reduce TOW to the estimate difference
nodes.statement: These expected rewards, $Q^{\prime}_j$s, are not the same as those given by the learning rules of TOW dynamics, $Q_j$s in Eq.(\ref{eq:org}). However, what we use substantially in TOW dynamics is the difference \begin{equation} Q_A - Q_B  =  (N_A - N_B) - (1 + \omega)\hspace{1mm}(L_A - L_B). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Observe that only the difference $Q_A - Q_B$ matters in TOW dynamics.

nodes.name: Rescale the imaginary estimates and take the difference
nodes.statement: When we transform the expected rewards $Q^{\prime}_j$s into $Q^{\prime \prime}_j  =  Q^{\prime}_j / (2 - \gamma)$, we can obtain the difference \begin{equation} Q^{\prime \prime}_A - Q^{\prime \prime}_B  =  (N_A - N_B) - \frac{2}{2-\gamma} \hspace{1mm} (L_A - L_B). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Divide by $2-\gamma$ to put the imaginary difference in the same form as the TOW difference.

nodes.name: Equivalence of the TOW learning rule to the simultaneous-update imaginary system
nodes.statement: Comparing the coefficients of Eq.(\ref{eq:dq}) and (\ref{eq:dqpp}), the differences in their constituent terms are always equal when $\omega=\omega_0$ (Eq.(\ref{eq:w0})) is satisfied. Eventually, we can obtain the nearly optimal weighting parameter $\omega_0$ in terms of $\gamma$. This derivation implies that the learning rule for TOW dynamics is equivalent to that of the imaginary system in which both of the two estimates can be updated simultaneously.
nodes.statement_short: At $\omega = \omega_0$ the TOW learning rule coincides with the imaginary system that updates both estimates at once.
assumptions: when $\omega=\omega_0$ (Eq.(\ref{eq:w0})) is satisfied
conclusions: the differences in their constituent terms are always equal
the learning rule for TOW dynamics is equivalent to that of the imaginary system in which both of the two estimates can be updated simultaneously

nodes.name: Origin of the high performance of TOW dynamics
nodes.statement: In other words, TOW dynamics imitates the imaginary system that determines its next move at time $t+1$ in referring to the estimates of the two machines, even if one of them was not actually played at time $t$. This unique feature in the learning rule, derived from the fact that the sum of reward probabilities is given in advance, may be one of the origins of the high performance of TOW dynamics.
nodes.statement_short: TOW effectively consults both machines' estimates each step, which may explain its high performance.

nodes.name: Monte Carlo verification of $\omega_0$
nodes.statement: Monte Carlo simulations were performed it was verified that TOW dynamics with $\omega_0$ exhibits an exceptionally high performance, which is comparable to its peak performance---achieved with the optimal parameter $\omega_{opt}$. To derive the optimal value $\omega_{opt}$ accurately, we need to take into account the fluctuation and other dynamics of terminals~\cite{kim4}.
nodes.statement_short: Simulations show $\omega_0$ nearly attains the peak performance reached at the optimal $\omega_{opt}$.

nodes.name: Generalized $\omega_0$ for $M$-machine cases
nodes.statement: In addition, the essence of the process described here can be generalized to $M$-machine cases. To separate distributions of the top $m$-th and top $(m+1)$-th machine, as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:random}(b), all we need is the following $\omega_0$: \begin{eqnarray} \omega_0  & = & \frac{\gamma^{\prime}}{2 - \gamma^{\prime}} , \\ \gamma^{\prime} & = & P_{(m)} + P_{(m+1)} \end{eqnarray} Here, $P_{(m)}$ denotes the top $m$-th reward probability.
nodes.statement_short: For $M$ machines, use $\omega_0 = \gamma'/(2-\gamma')$ with $\gamma'$ the sum of the top $m$-th and $(m+1)$-th reward probabilities.
assumptions: To separate distributions of the top $m$-th and top $(m+1)$-th machine

nodes.name: Social maximum for $M$-machine and $X$-player cases
nodes.statement: In fact, for $M$-machine and $X$-player cases, we have designed a physical system that can  determine the overall optimal state, called the ``social maximum,'' quickly and accurately~\cite{bom}.

nodes.name: cheater algorithm
nodes.statement: To further investigate the origins of the high performance of TOW dynamics, let us consider another imaginary model for solving the MBP, called the ``cheater algorithm.'' The cheater algorithm selects a machine to play according to the following estimate $S_k$ ($k\in \{A,B\}$) \begin{eqnarray} S_A  & = & X_{A, 1} + X_{A, 2}, + \cdots + X_{A, N} , \\ S_B  & = & X_{B, 1} + X_{B, 2}, + \cdots + X_{B, N} . \end{eqnarray} Here, $X_{k, i}$ is a random variable that takes either $1$ (rewarded) or $0$ (non-rewarded). If $S_A$ $>$ $S_B$ at time $t=N$, machine $A$ is played at time $t=N+1$. If $S_B$ $>$ $S_A$ at time $t=N$, machine $B$ is played at time $t=N+1$. If $S_A$ $=$ $S_B$ at time $t=N$, a machine is played randomly at time $t=N+1$. Note that the algorithm refers to results of both machines at time $t$ without any attention to which machine was played at time $t-1$. In other words, the algorithm ``cheats'' because it plays both machines and collects both results, but declares that it plays only one machine at a time.
nodes.statement_short: An idealized reference policy that secretly observes both machines' reward streams and plays whichever has the larger cumulative sum.
input: $X_{k, i}$ is a random variable that takes either $1$ (rewarded) or $0$ (non-rewarded)

nodes.name: Accumulate both reward sums
nodes.statement: The cheater algorithm selects a machine to play according to the following estimate $S_k$ ($k\in \{A,B\}$) \begin{eqnarray} S_A  & = & X_{A, 1} + X_{A, 2}, + \cdots + X_{A, N} , \\ S_B  & = & X_{B, 1} + X_{B, 2}, + \cdots + X_{B, N} . \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Sum the $0/1$ reward variables of both machines up to time $N$.

nodes.name: Branch when $S_A > S_B$
nodes.statement: If $S_A$ $>$ $S_B$ at time $t=N$, machine $A$ is played at time $t=N+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Play $A$ when its sum is larger.

nodes.name: Branch when $S_B > S_A$
nodes.statement: If $S_B$ $>$ $S_A$ at time $t=N$, machine $B$ is played at time $t=N+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Play $B$ when its sum is larger.

nodes.name: Random tie-break
nodes.statement: If $S_A$ $=$ $S_B$ at time $t=N$, a machine is played randomly at time $t=N+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Break ties uniformly at random.

nodes.name: Gaussian statistics of the cheater estimates $S_k$ and $S = S_A - S_B$
nodes.statement: The expected value and the variance of $X_k$ are defined as $E (X_k)  =  \mu_k $ and $V (X_k)  =  \sigma_k^{2}$. Here, $\mu_k$ is the same as the $P_k$ defined earlier. From the central-limit theorem, $S_k$ has a Gaussian distribution with $E (S_k)  =  \mu_k N$ and $V (S_k)  =  \sigma_k^{2} N$. If we define a new variable $S = S_A - S_B$, $S$ has a Gaussian distribution and carries the following values: \begin{eqnarray} E (S)  & = & (\mu_A + \mu_B) N  ,\\ V (S)  & = & (\sigma_A^{2} +  \sigma_B^{2}) N ,\\ \sigma (S)  & = & \sqrt{ \sigma_A^{2} +  \sigma_B^{2}} \sqrt{N} . \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: By the central-limit theorem the cheater sums, and their difference $S$, are Gaussian with mean and variance linear in $N$.
assumptions: The expected value and the variance of $X_k$ are defined as $E (X_k)  =  \mu_k $ and $V (X_k)  =  \sigma_k^{2}$.
From the central-limit theorem
If we define a new variable $S = S_A - S_B$
conclusions: $S_k$ has a Gaussian distribution with $E (S_k)  =  \mu_k N$ and $V (S_k)  =  \sigma_k^{2} N$

nodes.name: Probability of selecting the lower-reward machine
nodes.statement: From Fig.~\ref{fig:Qfunc}, the probability of playing machine $B$, which has a lower reward probability, can be described as {\bf Q}$(\frac{E(S)}{\sigma(S)})$. Here, {\bf Q}$(x)$ is a {\bf Q}-function. We obtain \begin{eqnarray} P(t=N+1,B) & = & {\bf Q}(\phi \sqrt{N}) . \end{eqnarray} Here, $\phi = \frac{\mu_A - \mu_B}{\sqrt{\sigma_A^2 + \sigma_B^2}}$.
nodes.statement_short: The cheater algorithm picks the worse machine with probability ${\bf Q}(\phi\sqrt{N})$, where $\phi$ is the normalized reward gap.
assumptions: the probability of playing machine $B$, which has a lower reward probability, can be described as {\bf Q}$(\frac{E(S)}{\sigma(S)})$
Here, $\phi = \frac{\mu_A - \mu_B}{\sqrt{\sigma_A^2 + \sigma_B^2}}$

nodes.name: Chernoff bound
nodes.statement: Using the Chernoff bound ${\bf Q}(x)  \leq  \frac{1}{2} \exp(-\frac{x^2}{2})$

nodes.name: regret
nodes.statement: we can calculate the upper bound of a measure, called the ``regret'', which quantifies the accumulated losses of the cheater algorithm. \begin{equation} regret = (\mu_A - \mu_B) E(N_B). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The regret is the reward gap times the expected number of plays of the inferior machine.
differentia: which quantifies the accumulated losses of the cheater algorithm

onumber \ & = &  rac{1}{2} + \Sigma_{t=1}^{N-1}  rac{1}{2} \exp(- rac{\phi^2}{2} t) 
onumber \ & \leq &  rac{1}{2} + \int_{0}^{N-1}  rac{1}{2} \exp(- rac{\phi^2}{2} t) dt 
onumber \ & = &  rac{1}{2} -  rac{1}{\phi^2} \left( \exp(- rac{\phi^2}{2}(N-1))  - 1  ight) \ & ightarrow &  rac{1}{2} +  rac{1}{\phi^2} . \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Sum the per-step error probabilities, bound each by the Chernoff bound, dominate the geometric sum by an integral, and let $N \to \infty$.

nodes.name: Expected plays of the inferior machine as a sum of Q-functions
nodes.statement: E(N_B) & = & \Sigma_{t=0}^{N-1} {\bf Q}(\phi \sqrt{t})
nodes.statement_short: Write $E(N_B)$ as the sum of the per-step selection probabilities.

nodes.name: Apply the Chernoff bound termwise
nodes.statement: & \leq & \Sigma_{t=0}^{N-1} \frac{1}{2} \exp(-\frac{\phi^2}{2} t)
nodes.statement_short: Replace each Q-function by its exponential Chernoff bound.

nodes.name: Split off $t=0$ and dominate the sum by an integral
nodes.statement: & = & \frac{1}{2} + \Sigma_{t=1}^{N-1} \frac{1}{2} \exp(-\frac{\phi^2}{2} t) \nonumber \\ & \leq & \frac{1}{2} + \int_{0}^{N-1} \frac{1}{2} \exp(-\frac{\phi^2}{2} t) dt
nodes.statement_short: Peel off the $t=0$ term and bound the remaining geometric sum by an integral.

nodes.name: Evaluate the integral and take the large-$N$ limit
nodes.statement: & = & \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{\phi^2} \left( \exp(-\frac{\phi^2}{2}(N-1))  - 1  \right) \\ & \rightarrow & \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\phi^2} .
nodes.statement_short: Integrate and conclude the bound tends to $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\phi^2}$.

nodes.name: Constant regret of the cheater algorithm
nodes.statement: Note that the regret becomes constant as $N$ increases.
assumptions: Using the Chernoff bound ${\bf Q}(x)  \leq  \frac{1}{2} \exp(-\frac{x^2}{2})$
$regret = (\mu_A - \mu_B) E(N_B)$
conclusions: the regret becomes constant as $N$ increases

nodes.name: Mean and variance of the TOW score difference $S$
nodes.statement: Using the ``cheated'' results, we can also calculate the regret of TOW dynamics in the same way. In this case, \begin{eqnarray} S_A  & = & X_{A, 1} + X_{A, 2}, + \cdots + X_{A, N_A} - \omega L_A , \\ S_B  & = & X_{B, 1} + X_{B, 2}, + \cdots + X_{B, N_B} - \omega L_B . \end{eqnarray} $X_{k, i}$ is also a random variable that takes either $1$ (rewarded) or $0$ (non-rewarded). Here, we use $L_k$$=$$(1 - \mu_k) N_k$. Then, we obtain $E (S_k)  =  \{ \mu_k - (1 - \mu_k) \omega \}  N_k$ and $V (S_k)  = \sigma_k^{2} N_k$. Using the new variables $S = S_A - S_B$, $N = N_A + N_N$, and $D = N_A - N_N$, we also obtain \begin{eqnarray} E (S)  & = & \frac{\mu_A - \mu_B}{2} (1 + \omega) N + \nonumber \\ &   & \{ \frac{\mu_A + \mu_B}{2} (1 + \omega) - \omega \} D   ,\\ V (S)  & = & \frac{\sigma_A^2 + \sigma_B^2}{2} N +  \frac{\sigma_A^2 - \sigma_B^2}{2} D . \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: For TOW scores with punishment weight $\omega$, the difference $S$ has mean and variance decomposed into a total-play part $N$ and an imbalance part $D$.
assumptions: $X_{k, i}$ is also a random variable that takes either $1$ (rewarded) or $0$ (non-rewarded)
Here, we use $L_k$$=$$(1 - \mu_k) N_k$
Using the new variables $S = S_A - S_B$, $N = N_A + N_N$, and $D = N_A - N_N$

nodes.name: TOW statistics and selection probability under $\omega = \omega_0$ and $\sigma_A = \sigma_B$
nodes.statement: If the conditions $\omega  = \omega_0$ and $\sigma_A = \sigma_B$ $\equiv \sigma$ are satisfied, we then obtain \begin{eqnarray} E (S)  & = & \frac{\mu_A - \mu_B}{2} (1 + \omega_0) N ,\\ V (S)  & = & {\sigma^2} N , \end{eqnarray} and \begin{eqnarray} P(t=N+1,B) & = & {\bf Q}(\phi_{T} \sqrt{N}) .    \end{eqnarray} Here, $\phi_{T} = \frac{(\mu_A - \mu_B) (1 + \omega_0)}{2 \sigma}$.
nodes.statement_short: At $\omega = \omega_0$ with equal variances, the $D$-dependent terms vanish and TOW picks the worse machine with probability ${\bf Q}(\phi_T\sqrt{N})$.
assumptions: $\omega  = \omega_0$
$\sigma_A = \sigma_B$ $\equiv \sigma$

nodes.name: Upper bound of the regret for TOW dynamics
nodes.statement: We can then calculate the upper bound of the regret for TOW dynamics \begin{eqnarray} E(N_B) & = & \Sigma_{t=0}^{N-1} {\bf Q}(\phi_{T} \sqrt{t}) \nonumber \\ & \leq & \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{\phi_{T}^2} \left( \exp(-\frac{\phi_{T}^2}{2}(N-1))  - 1  \right) \\ & \rightarrow & \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\phi_{T}^2} . \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Repeat the cheater-algorithm Chernoff-plus-integral bound with $\phi$ replaced by $\phi_T$.

nodes.name: Bound the sum of Q-functions at $\phi_T$
nodes.statement: E(N_B) & = & \Sigma_{t=0}^{N-1} {\bf Q}(\phi_{T} \sqrt{t}) \nonumber \\ & \leq & \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{\phi_{T}^2} \left( \exp(-\frac{\phi_{T}^2}{2}(N-1))  - 1  \right)
nodes.statement_short: Apply the same Chernoff-and-integral estimate with $\phi_T$.

nodes.name: Take the large-$N$ limit
nodes.statement: & \rightarrow & \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\phi_{T}^2} .
nodes.statement_short: Conclude the bound converges to $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\phi_T^2}$.

nodes.name: Constant regret of TOW dynamics
nodes.statement: Note that the regret for TOW dynamics also becomes constant as $N$ increases.
assumptions: If the conditions $\omega  = \omega_0$ and $\sigma_A = \sigma_B$ $\equiv \sigma$ are satisfied
$regret = (\mu_A - \mu_B) E(N_B)$
conclusions: the regret for TOW dynamics also becomes constant as $N$ increases

nodes.name: Logarithmic regret of optimal MBP algorithms
nodes.statement: It is known that optimal algorithms for the MBP, defined by Auer et al., have a regret proportional to $\log(N)$. The regret has no finite upper bound as $N$ increases because it continues to require playing the lower-reward machine to ensure that the probability of incorrect judgment goes to zero.
nodes.statement_short: Optimal MBP algorithms have $\log(N)$ regret, which is unbounded because they must keep sampling the inferior machine.
assumptions: optimal algorithms for the MBP, defined by Auer et al.
conclusions: The regret has no finite upper bound as $N$ increases because it continues to require playing the lower-reward machine to ensure that the probability of incorrect judgment goes to zero

nodes.name: Practical interpretation of constant regret
nodes.statement: A constant regret means that the probability of incorrect judgment remains non-zero in TOW dynamics, although this probability is nearly equal to zero. However, it would appear that the reward probabilities change frequently in actual decision-making situations, and their long-term behavior is not crucial for many practical purposes. For this reason, TOW dynamics would be more suited to real-world applications.
nodes.statement_short: Constant regret leaves a tiny non-zero error probability, which matters little in non-stationary real-world settings.

nodes.name: Efficient decision-making is embedded in any volume-conserving physical object
nodes.statement: In this Letter, we proposed TOW dynamics for solving the MBP and analytically validated that their high efficiency in making a series of decisions for maximizing the total sum of stochastically obtained rewards is embedded in any volume-conserving physical object when subjected to suitable operations involving fluctuations.
nodes.statement_short: The analysis shows that TOW's decision-making efficiency is intrinsic to any volume-conserving object driven by fluctuating operations.
assumptions: in any volume-conserving physical object when subjected to suitable operations involving fluctuations
conclusions: their high efficiency in making a series of decisions for maximizing the total sum of stochastically obtained rewards is embedded in any volume-conserving physical object

nodes.name: Novelty of the sum-based weighting parameter $\omega_0$
nodes.statement: In conventional decision-making algorithms for solving the MBP, the parameter for adjusting the ``exploration time'' must be optimized. This exploration parameter often reflects the difference between the rewarded experiences, i.e., $|P_A - P_B |$. In contrast, TOW dynamics demonstrates that a higher performance can be achieved by introducing a weighting parameter $\omega_0$ that refers to the sum of the rewarded experiences, i.e., $P_A$ $+$ $P_B$. Owing to this novelty, the high performance of TOW dynamics can be reproduced when implementing these dynamics with various volume-conserving physical objects. Thus, our proposed physics-based analog-computing paradigm would be useful for a variety of real-world applications and for understanding the biological information-processing principles that exploit their underlying physics.
nodes.statement_short: Conventional exploration parameters track the reward difference, whereas TOW's $\omega_0$ tracks the reward sum, which is what makes it physically reproducible.
